Spotted thick-knee (Burhinus capensis) exhibits a notable oviparous reproductive strategy characteristic of the Charadriiformes order. Eggs are deposited in shallow scrapes on open ground, and artificial incubation data suggest an optimal temperature for embryogenesis of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], under which hatching occurs after an incubation period of approximately 27 days [ab = approximately 27 days]. Newly emerged chicks are semi-precocial, weighing roughly 22 grams [Wwb = roughly 22 grams] upon hatching, a modest mass that facilitates rapid mobility for foraging alongside attentive parents. This neonatal body size is comparable to values reported for other congeners, reflecting a developmental pathway balanced between yolk investment and post-hatching parental provisioning. Following hatching, the downy chicks are brooded regularly during the first few days but begin pecking at small invertebrates within hours of leaving the nest. The relatively short incubation period allows breeding pairs to capitalise on seasonal prey pulses, though it also imposes high thermal demands on the incubating adult to maintain steady egg temperatures well above ambient in the cool nocturnal environments the species often occupies.

The time since birth at fledging is approximately 55 days [tx = approximately 55 days], a period during which flight feathers mature and the chick gains sufficient wing loading for sustained, evasive flight away from terrest at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]rial predators. This relatively protracted nestling phase, compared to some smaller wader species, reflects the energetic demands of achieving a large adult body size from a modest neonatal start. Parents continue to provision the fledgling for several weeks after nest departure, with the young bird gradually learning to capture grasshoppers, beetles, and other arthropods independently. Field observations indicate that the post-fledging dependency period is critical for honing foraging skills in the thorny savanna habitats the species prefers. Mortality during this phase is relatively high, with predation from raptors and mammalian carnivores accounting for a substantial proportion of losses before the young bird reaches independence.

Onset of reproductive maturity in Spotted thick-knee is delayed relative to many other charadriiform birds of comparable body mass. The time since birth at puberty, defined as the point at which gonadal maturation is first detectable, occurs at approximately 165 days [tp = approximately 165 days] in individuals maintained at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This relatively late maturation is likely linked to the extended period required for young birds to acquire sufficient somatic reserves and foraging proficiency necessary for successful territory defence and pair bonding. The species typically delays actual reproduction further, with the time since birth at first brood estimated at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when measured under similar thermal conditions at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This gap between physiological puberty and first successful reproduction is common among long-lived bird species, allowing juveniles to refine courtship behaviours and secure high-quality nesting territories in competitive landscapes dominated by older, experienced adults.

Adult females of Spotted thick-knee attain a maximum body mass of approximately 490 grams [Wwi = approximately 490 grams], a value placing the species among the heavier members of the Burhinidae family. This ultimate wet weight for females is achieved after a gradual growth trajectory that continues well beyond the fledging period, with individuals often not reaching asymptotic mass until their second or third year of life. The substantial mass supports the species' omnivorous diet, which includes large insects, small vertebrates, and occasional plant material, providing the energetic reserves needed for prolonged egg incubation and chick guarding. In terms of reproductive output, females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing between one and three eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing between one and three eggs], though two is the most common count. This modest laying frequency results in a maximum annual egg production of approximately two eggs per year [Ri = approximately two eggs per year], a rate consistent with the species' K-selected life history strategy that emphasises offspring survival over numerical output.

Longevity in Spotted thick-knee, though challenging to estimate from wild populations due to high adult mortality, has been inferred from data on the closely related Burhinus oedicnemus, for which the lifespan at 40.9 °C is approximately 17.8 years [am = approximately 17.8 years] at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This extended lifespan, exceeding many other wader species of comparable size, aligns with the delayed reproduction and low annual fecundity documented above. Individuals surviving the vulnerable juvenile and early adult years can enjoy multiple reproductive seasons, likely contributing substantially to the population's recruitment over a protracted adult life stage. The species' cryptic plumage and nocturnal activity patterns reduce predation risk for experienced adults, while their habit of freezing rather than fleeing when disturbed likely conserves energy during non-breeding periods. Overall, the life history of Burhinus capensis exemplifies a slow pace-of-life syndrome, characterised by late maturation, long potential lifespan, and a conservative reproductive output that buffers against environmental stochasticity in the semi-arid savanna ecosystems it inhabits.
